subject: religious-studies
topicDisplay: Religious & Ethical Teachings about Crime & Punishment
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of the following is most commonly identified by religious believers as a social cause of crime?
questions.explain: Poverty is widely taught as a driver of crime because deprivation can push people to steal to survive.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a psychological or personal cause of crime?
questions.explain: Mental illness and addiction are recognised personal factors that can lead individuals into crime.

questions.q: Some people break the law because they oppose a law they see as unjust. This cause of crime is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: People sometimes break laws they consider morally wrong, such as protesters against apartheid or discrimination.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the recognised aims of punishment?
questions.explain: Deterrence is an aim of punishment intended to put people off committing crimes.

questions.q: The aim of punishment that focuses on making the offender pay for their wrongdoing, often linked to 'an eye for an eye', is called what?
questions.explain: Retribution treats punishment as the offender getting what they deserve for their crime.

questions.q: Which aim of punishment is concerned with changing the offender so that they do not commit crimes again?
questions.explain: Reformation aims to help the offender change for the better and become a law-abiding citizen.

questions.q: The aim of punishment that seeks to keep society safe from a dangerous criminal is known as which of the following?
questions.explain: Protection aims to keep the public safe, often by removing the offender from society through imprisonment.

questions.q: In the Bible, the teaching 'an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth' is found in which book?
questions.explain: The principle of equivalent retribution appears in the Old Testament book of Exodus.

questions.q: Which international organisation campaigns against the use of the death penalty worldwide?
questions.explain: Amnesty International is a human rights organisation that campaigns for the abolition of the death penalty.

questions.q: Jesus told Peter to forgive not seven times but how many, emphasising limitless forgiveness?
questions.explain: Jesus taught forgiveness 'seventy-seven times' (or seventy times seven) to show it should have no limit.

questions.q: The saying 'Let him who is without sin cast the first stone' is used by many Christians to support which idea?
options: Showing mercy and not condemning others
questions.explain: Jesus' words when the woman was about to be stoned are used to argue for mercy over harsh punishment.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key Christian argument AGAINST the death penalty?
options: Life is sacred and given by God
It follows 'an eye for an eye'
questions.explain: Many Christians oppose capital punishment because of the sanctity of life, believing only God should end a life.

questions.q: Which argument is often used by those who SUPPORT the death penalty?
options: It acts as a strong deterrent to serious crime
It protects the sanctity of life
It allows the offender to reform
questions.explain: Supporters argue the death penalty deters others from committing the most serious crimes such as murder.

questions.q: A judge orders an offender to repair the damage they caused and compensate the victim. This best reflects which aim of punishment?
questions.explain: Reparation aims to put right the harm done and make amends to the victim or community.

questions.q: Why might a difficult upbringing be considered a cause of crime?
options: A child may learn criminal behaviour or lack positive role models
It guarantees the person becomes religious
It removes all responsibility from society
questions.explain: A poor upbringing can expose a child to crime or fail to teach right from wrong, increasing the risk of offending.

questions.q: Which statement best explains how deterrence is meant to work?
options: Fear of punishment discourages people from committing crimes
Offenders are helped to change their character
Society is kept safe by locking criminals away
Victims are compensated for their loss
questions.explain: Deterrence relies on the threat of punishment making people less likely to break the law.

questions.q: Many Christians believe forgiveness is important because of teaching in which prayer that links being forgiven with forgiving others?
questions.explain: The Lord's Prayer asks God to 'forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us'.

questions.q: A dangerous violent offender is given a long prison sentence mainly so the public cannot be harmed by them. Which aim of punishment is this?
questions.explain: Removing a dangerous person from society to keep others safe is the aim of protection.

questions.q: A prison offers education and therapy so that inmates can return to society as changed, law-abiding people. Which aim does this reflect?
questions.explain: Providing education and rehabilitation to change offenders for the better reflects the aim of reformation.

questions.q: A Christian whose family member was murdered chooses to forgive the killer rather than seek revenge. Which teaching most directly supports this response?
options: Jesus' teaching to love your enemies and forgive
'An eye for an eye' from Exodus
The argument that criminals cannot change
questions.explain: Jesus taught followers to love their enemies and forgive, which motivates some Christians to forgive even serious wrongdoing.
